claims.text: Annealing TaNbHfZrTi at approximately 0.5Tm for 1 hour followed by rapid quenching will induce nanoscale chemical clustering.
Nanoscale chemical clustering reduces the effective density of states at the Fermi level.
Nanoscale chemical clustering enhances impurity electron scattering.
The clustering-induced electronic changes diminish electron–phonon coupling.
Diminished electron–phonon coupling lowers Tc relative to the homogeneous as-cast state.
The as-cast, rapidly solidified TaNbHfZrTi material is a fully random solid solution with a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Local chemical clustering produces local variations in the electronic density of states.
Electron–phonon coupling is relevant to superconductivity in the studied class of HEAs.
Increased clustering disrupts spatially uniform superconductivity.
Annealed samples containing more nanoscale clustering will have a lower Tc than the as-cast baseline.
Annealed samples containing more nanoscale clustering will have a broader superconducting transition than the as-cast baseline.
Strong compositional disorder can be associated with suppression of superconductivity near an Anderson quantum phase transition.
The proposed clustering effect should be significant only when annealing avoids large-scale grain growth and phase separation.
The hypothesis is restricted to HEA systems in which electron–phonon coupling is the dominant superconducting mechanism.
TEM and APT can be used to quantify cluster size distributions and cluster volume fractions.
Specific-heat measurements can be used to estimate the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Unchanged Tc and transition sharpness despite demonstrably enhanced clustering would falsify the proposed clustering-controlled mechanism.
A lack of correlation between measured clustering metrics and superconducting properties would falsify the hypothesis.
